content_groups.group_title: Q4. Does uterine rupture always cause vaginal bleeding?

blocks.text: No. Significant haemorrhage may be concealed intra-abdominally.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What is the definitive management?

blocks.text: Emergency laparotomy with delivery and control of haemorrhage.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. Can the uterus always be repaired?

blocks.text: No. Repair depends on the extent and location of the rupture, haemorrhage, tissue condition and maternal circumstances.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. When might hysterectomy be required?

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What is a classical Caesarean scar?

blocks.text: A vertical incision through the upper uterine segment, associated with a substantially higher risk of rupture in subsequent labour.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What should you do if you suspect rupture during TOLAC?

blocks.text: Call senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams, resuscitate, alert theatre and blood bank, assess fetal status, and proceed to emergency laparotomy without unnecessary delay.

blocks.text: “A woman with a previous Caesarean suddenly develops fetal bradycardia and maternal shock. What do you do?”

“I am highly concerned about uterine rupture. I would immediately call the senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, theatre and neonatal teams and activate the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol. I would commence ABCDE resuscitation, obtain two large-bore IV accesses, send urgent bloods and arrange blood products. I would continuously assess the fetal and maternal condition but would not delay definitive treatment for unnecessary investigations. The patient requires emergency laparotomy for delivery and control of haemorrhage, with uterine repair or hysterectomy depending on the extent of the rupture and the clinical situation.”
Previous Caesarean + sudden fetal bradycardia + loss of station ± maternal shock = UTERINE RUPTURE until proven otherwise.
